1303.title: Signs of the times (Gaudium et Spes)
1303.hook: the Church reads events in the light of the gospel
1303.howItsDone: Catholic parishes, schools and justice groups often use Gaudium et Spes to reflect on current events, and the method of looking closely and then reading events in the light of the gospel is used in Catholic social action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pacem in Terris: rights with duties beside them, and peace standing on truth, justice, charity and freedom. Your line was peace on earth.

Red sky at night. People have read the weather off the sky for a long time, and in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus's critics can do it too. A red evening, fair weather tomorrow. A red and gloomy morning, a storm. Then he turns it on them. In the Douay-Rheims: "You know then how to discern the face of the sky: and can you not know the signs of the times?" You can read clouds. Can you read what's happening in front of you? That phrase turns up again in a document of the Second Vatican Council.
screen: `A RED SKY.` → `YOU CAN READ THE CLOUDS.` → `CAN YOU READ THE TIMES?`

segments.voice: First, where the document starts. Its Latin name, Gaudium et Spes, means joy and hope, and it opens there. The joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of people today, especially the poor and anyone who suffers, are, it says, the joys and hopes, griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ. Nothing genuinely human fails to find an echo in their hearts. The Church doesn't stand outside the world taking notes. It begins inside it. Second, the job. Early on comes the line our word lives in: the Church has the duty of scrutinizing the signs of the times and interpreting them in the light of the gospel. Two moves. Look closely, and don't flinch. Then read what you see by a particular light. Third, what reading is not. A sign of the times isn't whatever is trending. The council speaks of discerning, in the events, needs and hopes of an age, which are true signs of God's presence and purpose. Some things in an age are signs of grace. Some are wounds. Reading means telling them apart, slowly, with the gospel open. Fourth, the kitchen table. Most mornings arrive with a phone full of news: a flood, a strike, a new law, a missing child. You can scroll past it all, or drown in it. Gaudium et Spes offers a third way: stop at one story, notice the people in it, and ask what the gospel sees there.
screen: `JOYS AND HOPES, GRIEFS AND ANXIETIES.` · `SCRUTINIZE, THEN INTERPRET.` · `NOT EVERY TREND IS A SIGN.` · then, large: `CAN YOU NOT KNOW THE SIGNS OF THE TIMES?`

segments.voice: Choose one news story you saw today, just one, and don't argue with it. Look first: who is grieving, who is hoping, who is missing from the picture? If you pray, bring those people before God by name or by place, and ask to see them as the gospel would; if you don't, let the story be about people rather than sides for a moment.
Signs of the times. Jesus's phrase in Matthew, taken up by the council: look closely at the events of an age, and read them in the light of the gospel. Today's word.
Your line: read the signs. Some are grace, and some are wounds. See you tomorrow.

1304.title: Populorum Progressio (1967)
1304.hook: Paul VI: development is the new name for peace
1304.howItsDone: Catholics often support development work through parish collections and Catholic aid agencies, and Populorum Progressio is a standard text in Catholic teaching on global poverty and fair trade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the signs of the times: look closely at events, then read them in the light of the gospel. Your line was read the signs.

Development is the new name for peace. It sounds like a line off a charity poster. It comes from a papal letter. Paul the Sixth wrote it near the end of Populorum Progressio, a letter on the development of peoples. The idea underneath fits in a lunch break. A world where some nations feast while others go hungry is not at peace, however quiet the borders look. If you want peace, the letter says in effect, help people grow. Today's word is that letter.
screen: `A LINE OFF A POSTER?` → `THE DEVELOPMENT OF PEOPLES.` → `NO PEACE BESIDE HUNGER.`

segments.voice: First, what development means here. Paul the Sixth insists it can't be measured by money alone. Real development has to promote the good of every person and of the whole person. Food, yes, and health, and work. But also learning, culture, friendship, prayer. Growth that fills the bank and empties the person isn't what he means. Second, a hard paragraph about property. Private property, the letter says, is not an absolute right with no conditions on it. No one may keep for their own exclusive use what they don't need, while others lack what they need to live. And it calls in a voice from the early Church, Saint Ambrose, who told the wealthy, roughly: when you give to the poor, you aren't giving them what's yours. You're handing back what is theirs. Third, nations, not just neighbors. The letter asks that what rich countries have beyond their needs be put at the service of poorer ones. Generosity becomes a question for whole peoples. Fourth, peace. Isaiah has a line, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the work of justice shall be peace." Paul the Sixth reads peace the same way. It isn't simply the absence of war. It gets built, day after day, by justice. That's how a letter about wells, schools and fair trade ends up talking about peace.
screen: `EVERY PERSON, AND THE WHOLE PERSON.` · `PROPERTY ISN'T AN ABSOLUTE RIGHT.` · `WHAT RICH NATIONS HAVE TO SPARE.` · then, large: `THE WORK OF JUSTICE SHALL BE PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one kind of work that helps people grow on their own terms: a well dug, a girl kept in school, a small loan for a market stall, a clinic open after dark. Don't pick the biggest; pick the one that moves you, hold the faces of the people it serves, and ask what you might give it: money, time, a voice. If you pray, hold that work before God.
Populorum Progressio. The development of peoples: Paul the Sixth's letter on the growth of every person and the whole person, and on peace built by justice. Today's word.
Your line: development is peace. Every person, and the whole person. Same time tomorrow.

1305.title: Medellín (1968)
1305.hook: Latin American bishops commit to the poor
1305.howItsDone: Many Catholic communities in Latin America and beyond draw on the Medellín documents in their work with the poor, through base communities, parish outreach and religious orders living in poor neighborhoods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Populorum Progressio: development of every person and the whole person, and peace built by justice. Your line was development is peace.

A city in the mountains of Colombia, and a meeting room full of bishops from across Latin America. Outside, their continent: grand cathedrals, and not far from the cathedral steps, families with very little. The question on the table was simple to ask and hard to answer. What should the Church look like in a place like this? Rich and distant, or close enough to share the same street? The documents they wrote there are known by the city's name. Today's word is Medellín.
screen: `A CITY IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `CATHEDRALS AND HUNGER.` → `WHAT SHOULD THE CHURCH LOOK LIKE?`

segments.voice: First, a text that sits close to their concern. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus reads from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Read beside Medellín, it sounds like a description of the Church's job, not only of Jesus's. Second, poverty, pulled apart. Their document on the poverty of the Church names three senses. Poverty as lack: not enough food, housing, schooling. That, they say, is an evil, and not something God wants. Spiritual poverty: an open, empty-handed trust in God, the poverty of the beatitudes. And poverty as a commitment: choosing, freely and out of love, to share the condition of the poor, to stand with them and work against what keeps them poor. Third, the turn toward themselves. The bishops asked their own Church to live more simply, to make its buildings, titles and ways of living plainer, and to be present where the poor are. Not a Church that hands things down to the poor from a height. A Church with the poor. Fourth, why it reaches past Latin America. Some readers trace the phrase from last week, the option for the poor, back to soil like this. Whatever the history, the shape works on any ordinary day: tell apart the poverty to fight, the poverty to welcome, and the poverty to choose.
screen: `ANOINTED TO PREACH TO THE POOR.` · `THREE KINDS OF POVERTY.` · `A CHURCH THAT LIVES SIMPLY.` · then, large: `NOT FOR THE POOR, BUT WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Picture the map, Mexico down through Central America, the islands, the long sweep of South America to its tip, and let a few names come: a city, a country, someone you know with family there. Then let faces come: the street vendor, the grandmother raising grandchildren, the priest or nun working in a poor barrio. If you pray, hold that whole continent before God, in Spanish or Portuguese if you know a prayer; if you don't, simply wish them well, one place at a time.
Medellín. The Colombian city where Latin American bishops met and committed the Church to stand with the poor, and to become poorer itself. Today's word.
Your line: with the poor. Alongside them, never above them, on the same street. Until tomorrow.

1306.title: Justice in the World (1971)
1306.hook: bishops say acting for justice is part of preaching the gospel
1306.howItsDone: Catholic justice and peace groups, parish social-concerns committees and religious orders often cite Justice in the World as a reason their work for justice belongs at the heart of their faith, not beside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Medellín: three kinds of poverty, and a Church that lives alongside the poor. Your line was with the poor.

Is working for justice part of the gospel? Or is it something a Christian does afterward, on their own time, once the real religious work is done? A synod of bishops, gathered in Rome, faced that question head on and answered in a single sentence. Not a footnote, not an appendix at the back, but near the front, where nobody could miss it. The document goes by a plain name. Today's word is Justice in the World.
screen: `PART OF THE GOSPEL, OR AFTER IT?` → `A SYNOD IN ROME.` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. The bishops wrote that action on behalf of justice, and taking part in transforming the world, appear to them as a constitutive dimension of preaching the gospel. Constitutive is the key word. It means part of what something is, the way flour is part of bread, not sprinkled on top. On this reading, preaching the gospel with no concern for justice would be preaching something less than the gospel. Second, an old line behind it. The prophet Micah sums up what God asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God." Judgment there means justice, doing right by people. It sits in the same breath as mercy and walking with God, not in a separate department. Third, a mirror. The bishops didn't only point outward. They wrote that anyone who dares to speak to others about justice must first be just in their eyes. So they turned to the Church's own house: how it pays the people who work for it, how it uses its property, how it treats people within its own walls. Fourth, the gap. The letter of James pictures a hungry, ill-clothed neighbor, and someone who says to them, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go in peace, be ye warmed and filled", and gives them nothing. Kind words, empty hands. Justice in the World says that gap is not small. Words of faith and acts of justice belong in the same sentence.
screen: `A CONSTITUTIVE DIMENSION.` · `DO JUSTICE, LOVE MERCY, WALK WITH GOD.` · `FIRST, BE JUST YOURSELF.` · then, large: `GO IN PEACE, BE YE WARMED AND FILLED.`

segments.voice: Look over your own day the way the bishops looked over their own house: is there someone you owe a fair share of the work, an honest answer, a bill you've been slow to pay, credit you let someone else miss? Don't pick something heroic; find one small unfairness, real and doable, that you could put right before tonight. If you pray, ask for the courage to do it; if you don't, simply decide.
Justice in the World. The synod document saying that acting for justice is a constitutive part of preaching the gospel, beginning with the Church's own house. Today's word.
Your line: justice is gospel. Flour in the bread, not sprinkled on top. Rest well.

1307.title: Laborem Exercens (1981)
1307.hook: John Paul II: work is for the person, not the person for work
1307.howItsDone: Catholics often draw on Laborem Exercens in labor ministry, in Catholic business ethics and in keeping Sunday as a day of rest, and the letter is a standard text in Catholic teaching on work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Justice in the World: acting for justice is part of preaching the gospel, starting at home. Your line was justice is gospel.

A field of grain on a sabbath. Jesus's disciples are hungry, and as they walk they pluck the heads of grain. Critics object: that's work, and it's the day of rest. In Mark's Gospel, Jesus flips the order. In the Douay-Rheims: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." The rule serves the person. This path met the heart of John Paul the Second's letter on human work with the carpenter of Nazareth. Today, the rest of that letter, Laborem Exercens, which makes the same flip about the job you go to on Monday. Work is for the person, not the person for work.
screen: `GRAIN ON THE SABBATH.` → `MADE FOR MAN.` → `WORK FOR THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: First, people before capital. Laborem Exercens says work has priority over capital: the money, machines, buildings and tools of a business. All of these are things, and things are meant to serve persons. The twist: the machines themselves are the fruit of earlier human work, the inheritance of generations of workers. Capital is work, piled up. So it makes no sense to let the pile rule the people. Second, the boss behind the boss. John Paul the Second distinguishes a direct employer, the one who signs your contract, from what he calls an indirect employer: the laws, governments, markets and international arrangements that shape what any direct employer can offer. Whether work treats people well depends on that whole web, not just on a kind manager. Third, the tiredness. The letter doesn't pretend work is always joyful. It's honest about sweat and toil. And it offers Christians a way to carry that: work as a share in God's activity as creator, and its hardness, borne patiently, as a share in Christ's cross. Not a reason to accept unjust conditions. A way to find meaning inside honest, hard days. Fourth, Monday. If work is for the person, then a person crushed by work has the order upside down, like a sabbath that starves the hungry. The person comes first: before the target, before the inbox, before the machine.
screen: `PEOPLE BEFORE CAPITAL.` · `THE BOSS BEHIND THE BOSS.` · `SWEAT, CREATION AND THE CROSS.` · then, large: `THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.`

segments.voice: For a moment, no task, no list, no planning tomorrow: notice where work lives in your body, the jaw, the shoulders, the eyes, the hands, and let each one go a little, in turn. If thoughts of what's undone arrive, let them stand outside the door; you are not a machine on pause, you are a person resting. If you pray, rest before God the way the sabbath invites; if you don't, simply rest.
Laborem Exercens. John Paul the Second's letter on human work: people before capital, a whole web of employers, and work made for the person. Today's word.
Your line: the person first. Capital is only work, piled up. See you tomorrow.

1308.title: Structures of sin (1987)
1308.hook: sin can be built into systems
1308.howItsDone: Catholics examine structures of sin in social-justice education, in parish advocacy on laws and policies, and sometimes in examinations of conscience that ask about a person's part in unjust systems as well as personal sins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laborem Exercens: people before capital, and work made for the person. Your line was the person first.

A man at a counter needs a bed for the night. The shelter needs to see an ID. The office that issues IDs needs a home address. He has no home address; that's why he's at the shelter. The clerk is polite. The man in line behind him is patient. Nobody in the room means him any harm, and still the door stays shut, the same way, for the next person too. Something is wrong, and it isn't sitting in any one heart in that room. It's built into the way things are set up. Today's word gives it a name: structures of sin.
screen: `NO ADDRESS, NO ID, NO BED.` → `NOBODY IN THE ROOM IS CRUEL.` → `THE WRONG IS BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. John Paul the Second used the phrase in a letter on social concern, Sollicitudo Rei Socialis. He meant habits, rules and arrangements in a society that keep producing harm, even when no one in particular is choosing harm today. Second, where they come from. These structures don't fall from the sky. They are rooted in personal sin, and always linked to the concrete choices of people: those who set them up, strengthen them, and make them hard to take apart. Once built, they spread, and become the soil for more sin. The Catechism says it in one breath: structures of sin are the expression and the effect of personal sins. Third, what feeds them. The letter names two attitudes: an all-consuming desire for profit, and a thirst for power that wants to impose its will on others, both at any price. Neither needs a villain twirling a mustache. A lot of ordinary people quietly sharing them is enough. Fourth, an old insight. The prophet Isaiah saw it, in the Douay-Rheims: "Woe to them that make wicked laws: and when they write, write injustice." Sin can be written down, filed and stamped. The teaching cuts both ways. A system doesn't excuse anyone's own choices. And being personally kind doesn't excuse ignoring the system. The letter's answer is conversion, and the solidarity from last week: a firm commitment to the good of all.
screen: `HARM BUILT INTO HOW THINGS ARE SET UP.` · `ROOTED IN PERSONAL CHOICES.` · `PROFIT AND POWER AT ANY PRICE.` · then, large: `WOE TO THEM THAT MAKE WICKED LAWS.`

segments.voice: Think through a normal day, a form you filled in, a line you stood in, a rule at work or school, and look for one place where the setup itself keeps hurting the same kind of people, whoever is on duty. Don't try to fix it; just see it clearly, then ask the harder question: where am I part of it, even a little, and where could I push back? If you pray, bring both to God.
Structures of sin. Ways a society is set up that keep producing harm, rooted in personal choices, fed by profit and power at any price. Today's word.
Your line: sin in systems. The wrong was built in. I'll be here tomorrow.

Systems sin on their own, so the people inside them carry no share of the blame at all.
Only the powerful sin; being kind in your own life is all that ordinary people owe.
chat.meaning: John Paul II taught that structures of sin are rooted in personal choices and keep producing harm. A system excuses no one, and kindness doesn't excuse ignoring it.

1309.title: Centesimus Annus (1991)
1309.hook: after communism falls: markets have value but also limits
1309.howItsDone: Catholics draw on Centesimus Annus in business ethics, economics courses at Catholic universities and in thinking about consumer choices, and it is often read together with Rerum Novarum.

segments.voice: Yesterday, structures of sin: harm built into how things are set up, rooted in human choices. Your line was sin in systems.

A price tag. Some things wear one easily: a loaf of bread, a used car, an hour of a plumber's time. Other things turn strange the moment someone sticks one on: a friendship, a vote, a child. John Paul the Second wrote a letter marking a hundred years since Rerum Novarum, after the communist governments of Eastern Europe had fallen. It could have handed down a simple verdict on which economic system had won. Instead it's more careful: the market is a real good, and the market has edges. Its name means the hundredth year. Today's word is Centesimus Annus.
screen: `SOME THINGS WEAR A PRICE TAG.` → `SOME THINGS NEVER SHOULD.` → `THE HUNDREDTH YEAR.`

segments.voice: First, what markets do well. The letter calls the free market an efficient way to use resources and meet needs. It praises initiative, enterprise and work, and says profit has a proper place, as a sign that a business is doing its job. Second, where markets stop. There are many human needs, the letter says, that the market can't meet, because the people who have them have nothing to pay with. And some goods, by their very nature, cannot and must not be bought or sold. It leaves the list open; a verdict in court might be one, a child's care another. Profit is a sign, but not the only sign. A business is first a community of people. Third, having and being. The letter warns about consumerism: not the wish to live better, which it calls good, but a way of life aimed at having more rather than being more. Jesus puts it bluntly in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "a man's life doth not consist in the abundance of things which he possesseth." Fourth, the big question. Is a free economy the answer? If it means freedom to work and do business, set inside a strong framework of law that serves the whole human person, yes. If it means an economy answerable to nothing but itself, no. A market inside a moral frame, not a market as the frame.
screen: `WHAT MARKETS DO WELL.` · `GOODS THAT MUST NOT BE BOUGHT.` · `HAVING MORE, OR BEING MORE.` · then, large: `NOT IN THE ABUNDANCE OF THINGS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next thing you're likely to buy, groceries, a gift, something in a cart, and hold it: who made it, and were they paid fairly? Do you need it, or does it promise to make you more than you are, and is there a way to buy it that serves people better? No guilt needed, just attention; if you pray, ask for a free heart toward things; if you don't, simply decide what you'll do.

Centesimus Annus. The hundredth year: markets have value, and limits. This week: read the signs, development is peace, with the poor, justice is gospel, the person first, sin in systems, markets have limits. Today's word.
Your line: markets have limits. Some goods were never for sale. That's the day.

chat.says: So is the Church for or against the free market?
options: It calls the market a real good, but says some goods must never be bought or sold.
Against it: the letter says profit is always a sign that someone is being exploited.
For it, with no limits: whatever people will pay for is fine, as long as it's legal.
chat.meaning: Centesimus Annus praises initiative and calls the market efficient, but warns that some goods must not be bought or sold: a market inside a moral frame.
